# SystemVerilog basics {#sec-sv-basics .unnumbered}

## Goal for this week

- Learn to read SystemVerilog by knowing exactly where the C-like syntax
  stops being a reliable guide
- Separate combinational logic (`always_comb`) from sequential logic
  (`always_ff`), and the assignment operator each one requires
- Recognize latch inference and reset styles on sight, before they show up
  as bugs in your own pipeline stages

## It looks like C. It isn't.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module weird (input  logic a, b,
              output logic y1, y2);
  assign y1 = a & b;
  assign y2 = a | b;
endmodule
```

**Discussion question:** which line executes first, the assignment to `y1`
or the assignment to `y2`?
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The snippet above is syntactically close enough to C that it is tempting to
read it top to bottom, one statement after another. That reading is wrong,
and it is the single most important thing to unlearn this week. A module is
not a function that runs once and returns — it is a piece of hardware that
exists for as long as the circuit is powered. `y1` and `y2` are not
computed "first" and "second"; they are two separate wires, each
continuously driven by its own gate, both existing simultaneously and
forever. There is no call stack, no return value, and no "after" — only
signals that settle to a value whenever their inputs change.

Every construct in this chapter is a variation on this same fact: SV syntax
borrows C's punctuation, but describes structure and behavior in time, not
a sequence of steps.
:::

## Signals vs. variables

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `logic` — a signal that remembers its last driven value
- Vectors: `logic [7:0] data;`
- `typedef enum` and `typedef struct packed` group related signals under a
  name
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A CS variable holds a value because you assigned it one; nothing drives it
otherwise. A `logic` signal in SV is closer to a wire with memory — it
holds whatever it was last driven to, by whichever `assign` or `always`
block is responsible for it, and it is an error (caught by simulation, not
always by synthesis) for more than one such block to drive it.

```systemverilog
typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE, RUN, DONE} state_t;

typedef struct packed {
  logic       valid;
  logic [7:0] data;
} packet_t;
```

`typedef enum` gives a set of named constants a single type, instead of
scattering magic numbers through the code. `typedef struct packed` bundles
related signals into one name that can travel through a module's ports or
a pipeline register as a single unit — you will see exactly this pattern
in `pipeline_pkg.sv` next chapter, where control signals are grouped this
way instead of being passed as individual wires.
:::

## Combinational logic: `always_comb`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (sel == 2'b00)      y = in0;
  else if (sel == 2'b01) y = in1;
  // missing: sel == 2'b10, 2'b11
end
```

**Discussion question:** what does synthesis have to build for `y` when
`sel` is `2'b10`?
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
An `always_comb` block re-evaluates itself immediately whenever any signal
it reads changes — closer to a spreadsheet formula that recalculates on
every input edit than to a function you call. Assignment inside it uses
`=` (blocking), read as "this is what the output equals right now," not
"do this step, then the next."

The example above is an incomplete 2-to-1-style decoder: two of the four
`sel` cases are unhandled. In a spreadsheet, an unhandled case would just
show a blank cell. In hardware, `y` cannot go blank — if no branch assigns
it, the only way to keep `y` at *some* value is to remember the previous
one. Synthesis does exactly that: it infers a latch. This is almost never
what you want in a synchronous design, and it is the most common bug
`always_comb` produces. The fix is always the same: every signal assigned
in an `always_comb` block must be assigned on *every* path through it —
in practice, an `else` or a `default` branch on every `if`/`case`.

The complete version of the simplest case, a 2-to-1 multiplexer, has no
missing branch and therefore synthesizes to pure combinational logic, with
no memory element anywhere (@fig-mux2):

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (sel) y = in1;
  else     y = in0;
end
```

![A 2-to-1 multiplexer: `sel` chooses which input appears at `y`.](../images/blocks/mux2.svg){#fig-mux2 width=45%}
:::

## Sequential logic: `always_ff`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  q <= d;   // non-blocking
end
```

- `always_comb` → blocking, `=`
- `always_ff` → non-blocking, `<=`
- No exceptions to this pairing
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
`always_ff` describes a block that updates only at a clock edge — a
register, not a formula. It uses `<=` (non-blocking assignment), which
reads as "at this clock edge, schedule this update," rather than `=`'s
"this is the value right now." The distinction matters the moment two
`always_ff` blocks depend on each other, which is exactly the situation
every pipeline register is in.

Consider two registers meant to swap values on the same clock edge:

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  a <= b;
  b <= a;
end
```

With non-blocking assignment, both right-hand sides are read using each
register's value *before* this clock edge, and both updates take effect
together — the swap works, matching what "on every clock edge, in
parallel" should mean. Replace `<=` with `=` and the second line reads the
value the first line just wrote, collapsing two parallel updates into a
sequential one — the swap silently fails, and nothing about the syntax
warns you. This is why the pairing on the previous slide has no
exceptions: `=` in combinational logic, `<=` in clocked logic, every time.
:::

## Reset styles

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
// Synchronous reset
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst) q <= '0;
  else     q <= d;
end
```

```systemverilog
// Asynchronous reset
always_ff @(posedge clk or posedge rst) begin
  if (rst) q <= '0;
  else     q <= d;
end
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Both styles produce a register that clears `q` to zero on reset; they
differ in *when* the clear can happen. A synchronous reset only takes
effect at a clock edge — `rst` is just another input to the same logic
that decides the next value of `q`. An asynchronous reset takes effect the
moment `rst` asserts, independent of the clock, which is why it appears in
the sensitivity list alongside `posedge clk`.

The DFF you will build next chapter as a pipeline register uses exactly
this pattern — it is worth being able to tell the two styles apart on
sight, since the choice affects how quickly a stalled or flushed pipeline
stage can be forced back to a known state.
:::

## From syntax to the pipeline

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
Next week: these constructs, applied to a real five-stage pipeline
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Every construct introduced in this chapter reappears immediately in the
next one. `typedef enum` and `typedef struct packed` are how
`pipeline_pkg.sv` groups control signals; `always_ff` with the
non-blocking assignment and reset style you just saw is how `if_id_reg`
and the other pipeline registers are built; `always_comb` with the
blocking assignment and complete-branch discipline is how the ALU and
decoder avoid the latch-inference trap. Nothing in the pipeline chapter
introduces new syntax — it only puts this chapter's syntax to work on a
larger example.
:::
